questions.q: What does "blast radius" refer to in the context of network segmentation?
options: The physical distance between a cloud region's data centers
The number of NSG rules attached to a single subnet
The cost impact of a denial-of-service attack
How much else an attacker can reach once a single resource is compromised
questions.explain: Blast radius describes exposure after a compromise — segmentation design is about limiting how far an attacker can move from one breached resource, not preventing the breach itself.

questions.q: Does VNet peering between an Azure hub and a spoke automatically force spoke-to-spoke traffic through the hub's firewall?
options: No — peering alone only connects the two peered VNets directly; forcing traffic through the hub requires user-defined routes on the spokes pointing at the firewall's private IP
Yes, every peered spoke automatically routes through whatever firewall exists in the hub
Yes, but only if both VNets are in the same subscription
No — peering actively blocks all traffic until an NSG explicitly allows it
questions.explain: Peering is just connectivity. Without a UDR on each spoke sending traffic to the firewall's private IP as next hop, spokes talk only to what they're directly peered to — nothing is implicitly routed through the hub.

questions.q: Why doesn't VPC peering scale well as an AWS hub-spoke mechanism for many VPCs?
options: VPC peering is deprecated and no longer supported
VPC peering doesn't transit — a peered to b peered to c does not let a reach c — and every pair needs its own peering connection, which is why Transit Gateway is used at scale instead
VPC peering can only connect VPCs in the same Availability Zone
VPC peering requires Network Firewall to be enabled first
questions.explain: Peering connections are point-to-point and non-transitive, so they don't scale to many VPCs the way a Transit Gateway's hub-and-spoke route tables do.

questions.q: In an AWS Transit Gateway design built to reproduce Azure's hub-spoke pattern, what should the route tables typically do?
options: Route every spoke VPC to every other spoke VPC directly, with no inspection point
Route each spoke VPC only to a shared inspection VPC, not directly to other spokes, so cross-workload traffic passes through a central chokepoint
Allow unrestricted routing by default, then add explicit deny rules afterward
Disable all routing between the Transit Gateway and any spoke VPC
questions.explain: Routing each spoke only to a shared inspection VPC (not spoke-to-spoke) reproduces the Azure hub-spoke pattern of forcing every cross-workload packet through a central chokepoint by default.

questions.q: Why is a separate AWS account or Azure subscription considered a stronger containment boundary than network segmentation alone?
options: Because accounts and subscriptions are always located in physically separate data centers
Because network segmentation is deprecated in both clouds

Because a compromised credential or role in one account/subscription generally cannot touch resources in a separate one by default, regardless of network connectivity, since IAM/RBAC trust doesn't cross that boundary
Because only one account or subscription per organization is allowed to run compute resources
questions.explain: Account and subscription boundaries are an identity/trust boundary, not just a network one — even a network design gap can't let a compromised identity in one account reach another account's resources by default.
